study.title: Psalm 6: cry for mercy and confidence in God's answer
study.overview: This psalm is an intense supplication of David amidst great physical, emotional and spiritual distress. He begins by asking that the Lord not discipline him in anger, describes his weakness and his crying, and ends with the confidence that God has heard his prayer and will make the enemies be ashamed. The text shows the passage from anguish to hope, without denying the pain, but giving it to God.

outline.title: Request for mercy in the midst of weakness
outline.explanation: David pleads not to be treated according to divine wrath, asks for healing and confesses that he is weakened and deeply troubled. The question - until when? expresses prolonged pain and the feeling of waiting without answer.

outline.title: Call for God's goodness and fear of death
outline.explanation: He asks that the Lord return to act on his behalf and the free, grounding his request on the goodness of God. The argument of the psalm is theological: in death there is no more visible praise to the Lord among the living, so the psalmist beg for restoration.

outline.title: Physical and emotional fear
outline.explanation: Suffering is described with strong images of tiredness, tears and eyes consumed by sadness. The pain is not only bodily; it reaches the closeness of the being and worsens before the opposition of the enemies.

outline.title: Certainty that God has heard and victory over enemies
outline.explanation: The turn of the psalm happens when David heads to the practitioners of wickedness and states that the Lord heard his voice, accepted his prayer, and will cause the adversaries to retreat and suddenly be ashamed.

study.context: The inscription features David as author and indicates the psalm for the regent, with string instruments and an eight-string harp, which suggests liturgical use. The commentators' notes consider that the occasion may have been a disease or deep inner anguish, but the text does not clearly define the exact moment.
study.theology: Psalm unites repentance, dependence on mercy and trust in the divine response. The request not to be punished in anger shows awareness that the human being cannot stand before God's holiness on his own merit. At the same time, David appeals to the goodness of the Lord, acknowledging that restoration comes from grace and not from the right. The mention of Xheol and death highlights the seriousness of distress, but the closure states that God hears the prayer of his servant. Theologically, the psalm teaches that lamentation can coexist with faith, and that the presence of God is the greatest good desired by the believer.

scholarViews.insight: The lament can reflect illness or great spiritual depression; at the end, the psalmist reaffirms his trust in the Lord.
There is a sudden change for the better: after crying and lamenting, the psalmist is confident that the outcome will be good.
The psalmist predicts that enemies will be ashamed and troubled; Clarke notes that Hebrew can also be read as a turn leading to repentance.

questions: What does this psalm teach about how to bring to God physical pain and inner distress at the same time?
How can David's confidence that God has heard his prayer strengthen faith when the answer is not yet visible?
How does the consciousness of God's mercy change the way we understand discipline, suffering, and repentance?
study.practice: Pray honestly when you are shot down, without hiding the pain or losing reverence. Bring to God both the suffering of the body and the sorrow of the soul, and ask for restoration based on his goodness, not on his own merit. If there is opposition or mockery, do not repay with bitterness; wait in the Lord and stand firm in the certainty that he hears prayer.
study.uncertainty: The commentators' note suggests possible causes for David's situation, such as illness or deep anguish, but the chapter does not accurately identify the occasion. There is also interpretive reading, and not absolute certainty, about details such as the relationship between suffering and sin and about the final nuance of some expressions in different translations.
